The concept of relativity, specifically time dilation, can be understood by comparing time to a rubber band. Imagine that time is not a rigid, unchanging ruler, but rather a stretchy material. When you are stationary or moving slowly, the rubber band stays at its normal length, and time passes at a steady, predictable rate. However, as you begin to move faster—especially approaching the speed of light—or as you enter a stronger gravitational field, the rubber band stretches.

For the person on the "train" moving at near-light speed, their local experience of time (the length of the rubber band right next to them) feels completely normal. They don't feel like they are moving in slow motion. But to an outside observer watching from a stationary position, the stretched rubber band means that the events happening on the fast-moving train are unfolding more slowly. It’s like watching a movie in slow motion; the actions are still happening, but they take much longer to complete from the perspective of the viewer. This illustrates how speed and gravity can warp the passage of time, making it relative rather than absolute.
